description: Horizon Atlas is a solo project exploring when sunlight and a clear view of Earth overlap at lunar landing sites. The interactive planner uses NASA terrain and orbital data to find windows for surface activities.
summary: Can an eight-hour activity on the Moon run while the Sun and Earth both clear the hills? Horizon Atlas compares three lunar sites using NASA observations and estimates the local skyline at two polar sites. Students and mission planners can change dates, observer height, and clearance, then find an uninterrupted window. Near the Odysseus landing site, an ideal horizon gives 20.4 hours of joint visibility over three days. Adding the modeled terrain reduces that to zero. Moving just one terrain-grid spacing can shift the first eight-hour window by hours.
details:
Horizon Atlas compares hourly Sun and Earth positions for three lunar sites using 2,163 site-time pairs from NASA/JPL Horizons. At two polar sites, it models the skyline from NASA LRO/LOLA elevations, tracing 720 bearings out to 120 km. A visitor can adjust an activity’s duration and visibility requirements, compare horizons, inspect four nearby positions, and export the observations. The planner works offline.

At the rounded Odysseus coordinates near Malapert A, the modeled skyline blocks sunlight throughout November 14–17, 2026. For a 2 m observer with zero additional clearance, the first eight-hour slot begins November 19 at 00:18 UTC. Across the central point and four 240 m offsets, the first starts span 16 h 50 min. This is an educational geometric estimate. Local obstacles, eclipses, power-system capacity and radio performance require separate analysis.

The application uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Node.js prepares the data. Twelve automated scientific tests include comparisons with raw NASA observations, a one-minute JPL crossing, and a synthetic obstructing ridge.

I used OpenAI Codex to help develop and build my idea. I directed the project and asked for a public website and an offline version. Codex selected NASA’s published challenge, proposed the terrain comparison and activity scheduling features, wrote and tested the software, and prepared the text and slides. NASA supplied the observations and elevation data.
